category: 2026 DRC-Uganda-France BDBV Outbreak (Active — PHEIC; deadliest and largest ever recorded in DRC; now spans 7 provinces)
killed: 3,475 confirmed DRC / 2 confirmed Uganda = 3,477 confirmed total
injured: 923 currently hospitalized in isolation (DRC, as of 12 September); Uganda outbreak closed with 18 recoveries
source: DRC situation update via ECDC (published 13-14 September) — data as of 12 September 2026
note: DRC: 7,200 confirmed cases across 62 of 167 mapped health zones in 7 provinces as of 12 September (published 13-14 September, +178 cases and +77 deaths since the 10 September report); 3,475 confirmed deaths; crude national CFR ~48.3%, but roughly 63.7% in North Kivu province (1,139 cases/725 deaths as of 9 September, most recent province breakdown available); 1,712 cumulative recoveries. DRC government spokesman Patrick Muyaya said the week's data shows the outbreak's growth 'peaked' in the third week of August, with 10 of the (then) 61 health zones going 21+ days without a new case — even as the outbreak keeps widening geographically, having reached a seventh province (Sud-Ubangi, western DRC) days earlier: a 23-year-old man who died in Gwaka on 9 September after a roughly three-week, 2,000km journey through South Kivu, Rwanda, Uganda, Ituri, Tshopo and Mongala; 38 of his contacts have been quarantined, per acting Sud-Ubangi governor Jean-René Galekwa Vundawe. Ebola cases were also detected among schoolchildren in Bunia, Ituri, as the 2026-27 school year opened. The outbreak has now surpassed the 2018-2020 Kivu epidemic's 3,317 cases to become the largest ever recorded in DRC, and per AP is tracking toward surpassing the 2014-16 West Africa epidemic's 11,310-death toll. Africa CDC officials warned 22 August that true case counts could be 2-3x higher (10,000-15,000) given official detection may capture only 30-40% of infections. Uganda: 20 confirmed cases (2 deaths, 18 recoveries) — declared over by its own Ministry of Health 28 July 2026 and confirmed over by WHO on 25 August after completing the 42-day monitoring period. France: 1 case, recovered and discharged 4 July, no secondary transmission. DRC and partners launched a revised 180-day, $1.3 billion response plan in Kinshasa on 4 September. A WHO Geneva briefing on 8 September said the response needs 1,600 more treatment beds (target 3,000, versus ~1,400 built across 59 treatment centers) and 5,000 more health workers (target 9,000 at 3 staff per bed, versus ~4,000 deployed). National contact-tracing coverage rose to 88% as of 12 September, up from 84.4% on 9 September, though community resistance — isolation refusals, unclaimed/untested bodies, a patient escape in North Kivu's Katwa health zone — continues to complicate follow-up in several provinces.
